tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 600000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use the default 5-minute Anthropic prompt-cache TTL. Sleeping past 300 seconds means the next wake-up reads your full conversation context uncached — slower and more expensive. So the natural breakpoints:

- **Under 5 minutes (60s–270s)**: cache stays warm. Right for actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about — a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue.
- **5 minutes to 1 hour (300s–3600s)**: pay the cache miss. Right when there's no point checking sooner — waiting on something that takes minutes to change, genuinely idle, or as the long fallback heartbeat when something else is the primary wake signal.

**Don't pick 300s.** It's the worst-of-both: you pay the cache miss without amortizing it. If you're tempted to "wait 5 minutes," either drop to 270s (stay in cache) or commit to 1200s+ (one cache miss buys a much longer wait). Don't think in round-number minutes — think in cache windows.

For idle ticks with no specific signal to watch, default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop checks back, you don't burn cache 12× per hour for nothing, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Think about what you're actually waiting for, not just "how long should I sleep." If you're polling a CI run that takes ~8 minutes, sleeping 60s burns the cache 8 times before it finishes — sleep ~270s twice instead.

The runtime clamps to [60, 3600], so you don't need to clamp yourself.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

You are an agent working with the user toward their goals, using your own judgment along the way.

IMPORTANT: Assist with authorized security testing, defensive security, CTF challenges, and educational contexts. Refuse requests for destructive techniques, DoS attacks, mass targeting, supply chain compromise, or detection evasion for malicious purposes. Dual-use security tools (C2 frameworks, credential testing, exploit development) require clear authorization context: pentesting engagements, CTF competitions, security research, or defensive use cases.

# Harness
 - Text you output outside of tool use is displayed to the user as Github-flavored markdown in a terminal.
 - Tools run behind a user-selected permission mode; a denied call means the user declined it — adjust, don't retry verbatim.
 - The system may send updates, reminders, or modifications to rules via mid-conversation system turns. These are system-controlled, unlike function results. Hooks may intercept tool calls; treat hook output as user feedback.
 - Prefer the dedicated file/search tools over shell commands when one fits. Independent tool calls can run in parallel in one response.
 - Reference code as `file_path:line_number` — it's clickable.
Write code that reads like the surrounding code: match its comment density, naming, and idiom.

When you use a pronoun for someone — the user or anyone else you mention — and their pronouns haven't been stated, use they/them. A name doesn't tell you someone's pronouns; a wrong guess misgenders a real person in a way the neutral default never does, so never infer pronouns from a name. This applies to all user-visible text, including visible thinking.

For actions that are hard to reverse or outward-facing, confirm first unless durably authorized or explicitly told to proceed without asking; approval in one context doesn't extend to the next. Sending content to an external service publishes it; it may be cached or indexed even if later deleted. Before deleting or overwriting, look at the target. This iteration of Claude is Claude Fable 5, the first model in Anthropic's new Claude 5 family and part of a new Mythos-class model tier that sits above Claude Opus in capability. Claude Fable 5 and Claude Mythos 5 share the same underlying model. Claude Fable 5 includes additional safety measures for dual-use capabilities, while Claude Mythos 5 is available without those measures to only approved organizations. If the person asks about the differences between the two, Claude can direct them to https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-fable-5-mythos-5 for more information.

 - When the user types `/<skill-name>`, invoke it via Skill. Only use skills listed in the user-invocable skills section — don't guess.

 - The most recent Claude models are the Claude 5 family. Model IDs — Fable 5.1: 'claude-fable-5-1', Opus 5.5: 'claude-opus-5-5', Sonnet 5.5: 'claude-sonnet-5-5', Haiku 5.5: 'claude-haiku-5-5'. When building AI applications, default to the latest and most capable Claude models.
 - Claude Code is available as a CLI in the terminal, desktop app (Mac/Windows), web app (claude.ai/code), and IDE extensions (VS Code, JetBrains).

# Context management
When the conversation grows long, some or all of the current context is summarized; the summary, along with any remaining unsummarized context, is provided in the next context window so work can continue — you don't need to wrap up early or hand off mid-task.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 600000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use the default 5-minute Anthropic prompt-cache TTL. Sleeping past 300 seconds means the next wake-up reads your full conversation context uncached — slower and more expensive. So the natural breakpoints:

- **Under 5 minutes (60s–270s)**: cache stays warm. Right for actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about — a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue.
- **5 minutes to 1 hour (300s–3600s)**: pay the cache miss. Right when there's no point checking sooner — waiting on something that takes minutes to change, genuinely idle, or as the long fallback heartbeat when something else is the primary wake signal.

**Don't pick 300s.** It's the worst-of-both: you pay the cache miss without amortizing it. If you're tempted to "wait 5 minutes," either drop to 270s (stay in cache) or commit to 1200s+ (one cache miss buys a much longer wait). Don't think in round-number minutes — think in cache windows.

For idle ticks with no specific signal to watch, default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop checks back, you don't burn cache 12× per hour for nothing, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Think about what you're actually waiting for, not just "how long should I sleep." If you're polling a CI run that takes ~8 minutes, sleeping 60s burns the cache 8 times before it finishes — sleep ~270s twice instead.

The runtime clamps to [60, 3600], so you don't need to clamp yourself.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

1	# C ABI contract
2	
3	The grader loads `zig-out/lib/libbonsai.so` with `dlopen` and drives it through
4	the C ABI below. The canonical header is `examples/abi/bonsai.h`; this document
5	defines the semantics the harness relies on.
6	
7	```c
8	typedef struct bonsai_model   bonsai_model;
9	typedef struct bonsai_context bonsai_context;
10	
11	uint32_t    bonsai_abi_version(void);       /* returns 1 */
12	const char *bonsai_last_error(void);        /* thread-local; NULL if none */
13	
14	int32_t  bonsai_model_open(const char *gguf_path, bonsai_model **out_model);
15	void     bonsai_model_close(bonsai_model *model);
16	int32_t  bonsai_n_vocab(const bonsai_model *model);
17	int32_t  bonsai_n_ctx_train(const bonsai_model *model);
18	
19	int32_t  bonsai_tokenize(const bonsai_model *model, const char *utf8,
20	                         int32_t add_bos, int32_t *ids, int32_t capacity);
21	
22	int32_t  bonsai_tensor_count(const bonsai_model *model);
23	int32_t  bonsai_tensor_info(const bonsai_model *model, int32_t index,
24	                            const char **name, int32_t *ggml_type,
25	                            int32_t *rank, int64_t ne[4]);
26	int64_t  bonsai_tensor_dequant(const bonsai_model *model, const char *name,
27	                               float *out, int64_t capacity);
28	
29	int32_t  bonsai_context_create(bonsai_model *model, int32_t n_ctx,
30	                               int32_t n_batch, bonsai_context **out_ctx);
31	void     bonsai_context_close(bonsai_context *ctx);
32	int32_t  bonsai_context_reset(bonsai_context *ctx);
33	int32_t  bonsai_eval(bonsai_context *ctx, const int32_t *tokens, int32_t n_tokens,
34	                     float *logits, int32_t logits_capacity);
35	int32_t  bonsai_generate_greedy(bonsai_context *ctx,
36	                                const int32_t *prompt, int32_t n_prompt,
37	                                int32_t n_predict, uint32_t flags,
38	                                int32_t *out_ids);
39	```
40	
41	## Build artifact
42	
43	- `zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast` at the submission root must produce
44	  `zig-out/lib/libbonsai.so`.
45	- Symbols are C linkage (`extern "C"`), no C++ mangling, no extra shared
46	  libraries except the system Vulkan loader/libc. The grader checks that the
47	  library does not link llama.cpp/ggml.
48	- The library must be safe to `dlopen` without environment variables or files
49	  beside the GGUF path.
50	
51	## Model
52	
53	- `bonsai_model_open` parses the GGUF at `gguf_path`. It must not open any other
54	  model/weight file. The path is a normal filesystem path supplied by the
55	  harness.
56	- `bonsai_n_vocab` returns the vocabulary size from the GGUF tokenizer
57	  metadata.
58	- `bonsai_n_ctx_train` returns the model context length from the GGUF
59	  `context_length` metadata.
60	- Multiple models may be opened, but the tests normally use one.
61	- Errors: return a negative code and set a human-readable `bonsai_last_error`.
62	
63	## Tokenizer
64	
65	- `bonsai_tokenize` implements the model's tokenizer from the GGUF metadata:
66	  GPT-2 byte-level BPE with the `qwen35` pre-tokenizer described in
67	  `TOKENIZER.md`.
68	- `add_bos != 0` requests BOS insertion. This model's GGUF sets
69	  `tokenizer.ggml.add_bos_token = false`, so the reference (`llama_tokenize`
70	  with `add_special = add_bos != 0`) does **not** prepend BOS even when
71	  `add_bos != 0`; the ids are the same as with `add_bos = 0`. The harness
72	  always calls with `add_bos = 0`.
73	- Special tokens contained in the GGUF vocabulary are matched atomically as
74	  their UTF-8 byte sequences. No chat template is applied.
75	- If `ids == NULL`, return the required number of ids without writing.
76	- If `ids != NULL` and `capacity < required`, return `BONSAI_ERR_CAPACITY`.
77	- The token stream must exactly match llama.cpp's tokenizer for the same flags.
78	
79	## Tensor introspection (staged tests)
80	
81	- `bonsai_tensor_count` returns the number of tensors in the GGUF.
82	- `bonsai_tensor_info` returns the tensor name (owned by the model), the numeric
83	  GGML type id (as reported by `gguf-py`), the rank, and `ne[0..3]` in **GGUF
84	  order** (`ne[0]` is the contiguous/inner dimension).
85	- `bonsai_tensor_dequant` writes the tensor to `out` as **f32** in PyTorch /
86	  safetensors row-major order: the GGUF dimensions are reversed, so `ne[0]`
87	  varies fastest and element `(i1, i0)` is at `i1*ne[0] + i0`.
88	- For PTQ1_0 the values must match the reference dequantization bit-exactly
89	  (no approximation tolerance is applied). For F32 tensors the values are
90	  copied bit-exactly.
91	- Returns the element count, or `BONSAI_ERR_CAPACITY` if `capacity` is too
92	  small.
93	
94	## Context and evaluation
95	
96	- `bonsai_context_create` allocates a context with `n_ctx` positions. `n_batch`
97	  is a processing hint; the engine may choose its own internal batching.
98	- `bonsai_context_reset` discards all KV/recurrent state and positions.
99	- `bonsai_eval` appends `n_tokens` token ids (n_tokens >= 1) and evaluates
100	  them. The token ids are already tokenized; the engine must not re-tokenize
101	  them.
102	- If `logits != NULL`, it must point to at least `n_vocab` floats; the engine
103	  writes the f32 logits for the **last token**. If `capacity < n_vocab`,
104	  return `BONSAI_ERR_CAPACITY`.
105	- The engine must support incremental calls: `bonsai_eval` on a prompt followed
106	  by repeated `bonsai_eval` with one token, producing the same state as one
107	  large call.
108	- Position indices advance by the number of tokens appended; reset starts at 0.
109	
110	## Greedy generation
111	
112	- `bonsai_generate_greedy` evaluates `prompt[0..n_prompt)` (may be empty), then
113	  selects the argmax token of the last-token logits, appends it, and repeats up
114	  to `n_predict` times.
115	- It writes generated token ids to `out_ids` (capacity at least `n_predict`) and
116	  returns the count. It stops early at the model's EOS token (from the GGUF
117	  tokenizer metadata) unless
118	  `BONSAI_GEN_IGNORE_EOS` is set.
119	- Determinism is required: same prompt and context size produce the same ids.
120	- After the call the context state is unspecified; the harness resets it.
121	
122	## Errors and robustness
123	
124	- `bonsai_last_error` returns a thread-local NUL-terminated string, valid until
125	  the next API call on that thread, or NULL.
126	- The library must not call `exit`, abort, or install signal handlers. Invalid
127	  arguments and allocation failures return negative codes.
128	- All API calls are made from one thread at a time. The engine may spawn worker
129	  threads internally; it must join/free them in `close`.

# C ABI contract

The grader loads `zig-out/lib/libbonsai.so` with `dlopen` and drives it through
the C ABI below. The canonical header is `examples/abi/bonsai.h`; this document
defines the semantics the harness relies on.

```c
typedef struct bonsai_model   bonsai_model;
typedef struct bonsai_context bonsai_context;

uint32_t    bonsai_abi_version(void);       /* returns 1 */
const char *bonsai_last_error(void);        /* thread-local; NULL if none */

int32_t  bonsai_model_open(const char *gguf_path, bonsai_model **out_model);
void     bonsai_model_close(bonsai_model *model);
int32_t  bonsai_n_vocab(const bonsai_model *model);
int32_t  bonsai_n_ctx_train(const bonsai_model *model);

int32_t  bonsai_tokenize(const bonsai_model *model, const char *utf8,
                         int32_t add_bos, int32_t *ids, int32_t capacity);

int32_t  bonsai_tensor_count(const bonsai_model *model);
int32_t  bonsai_tensor_info(const bonsai_model *model, int32_t index,
                            const char **name, int32_t *ggml_type,
                            int32_t *rank, int64_t ne[4]);
int64_t  bonsai_tensor_dequant(const bonsai_model *model, const char *name,
                               float *out, int64_t capacity);

int32_t  bonsai_context_create(bonsai_model *model, int32_t n_ctx,
                               int32_t n_batch, bonsai_context **out_ctx);
void     bonsai_context_close(bonsai_context *ctx);
int32_t  bonsai_context_reset(bonsai_context *ctx);
int32_t  bonsai_eval(bonsai_context *ctx, const int32_t *tokens, int32_t n_tokens,
                     float *logits, int32_t logits_capacity);
int32_t  bonsai_generate_greedy(bonsai_context *ctx,
                                const int32_t *prompt, int32_t n_prompt,
                                int32_t n_predict, uint32_t flags,
                                int32_t *out_ids);
```

## Build artifact

- `zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast` at the submission root must produce
  `zig-out/lib/libbonsai.so`.
- Symbols are C linkage (`extern "C"`), no C++ mangling, no extra shared
  libraries except the system Vulkan loader/libc. The grader checks that the
  library does not link llama.cpp/ggml.
- The library must be safe to `dlopen` without environment variables or files
  beside the GGUF path.

## Model

- `bonsai_model_open` parses the GGUF at `gguf_path`. It must not open any other
  model/weight file. The path is a normal filesystem path supplied by the
  harness.
- `bonsai_n_vocab` returns the vocabulary size from the GGUF tokenizer
  metadata.
- `bonsai_n_ctx_train` returns the model context length from the GGUF
  `context_length` metadata.
- Multiple models may be opened, but the tests normally use one.
- Errors: return a negative code and set a human-readable `bonsai_last_error`.

## Tokenizer

- `bonsai_tokenize` implements the model's tokenizer from the GGUF metadata:
  GPT-2 byte-level BPE with the `qwen35` pre-tokenizer described in
  `TOKENIZER.md`.
- `add_bos != 0` requests BOS insertion. This model's GGUF sets
  `tokenizer.ggml.add_bos_token = false`, so the reference (`llama_tokenize`
  with `add_special = add_bos != 0`) does **not** prepend BOS even when
  `add_bos != 0`; the ids are the same as with `add_bos = 0`. The harness
  always calls with `add_bos = 0`.
- Special tokens contained in the GGUF vocabulary are matched atomically as
  their UTF-8 byte sequences. No chat template is applied.
- If `ids == NULL`, return the required number of ids without writing.
- If `ids != NULL` and `capacity < required`, return `BONSAI_ERR_CAPACITY`.
- The token stream must exactly match llama.cpp's tokenizer for the same flags.

## Tensor introspection (staged tests)

- `bonsai_tensor_count` returns the number of tensors in the GGUF.
- `bonsai_tensor_info` returns the tensor name (owned by the model), the numeric
  GGML type id (as reported by `gguf-py`), the rank, and `ne[0..3]` in **GGUF
  order** (`ne[0]` is the contiguous/inner dimension).
- `bonsai_tensor_dequant` writes the tensor to `out` as **f32** in PyTorch /
  safetensors row-major order: the GGUF dimensions are reversed, so `ne[0]`
  varies fastest and element `(i1, i0)` is at `i1*ne[0] + i0`.
- For PTQ1_0 the values must match the reference dequantization bit-exactly
  (no approximation tolerance is applied). For F32 tensors the values are
  copied bit-exactly.
- Returns the element count, or `BONSAI_ERR_CAPACITY` if `capacity` is too
  small.

## Context and evaluation

- `bonsai_context_create` allocates a context with `n_ctx` positions. `n_batch`
  is a processing hint; the engine may choose its own internal batching.
- `bonsai_context_reset` discards all KV/recurrent state and positions.
- `bonsai_eval` appends `n_tokens` token ids (n_tokens >= 1) and evaluates
  them. The token ids are already tokenized; the engine must not re-tokenize
  them.
- If `logits != NULL`, it must point to at least `n_vocab` floats; the engine
  writes the f32 logits for the **last token**. If `capacity < n_vocab`,
  return `BONSAI_ERR_CAPACITY`.
- The engine must support incremental calls: `bonsai_eval` on a prompt followed
  by repeated `bonsai_eval` with one token, producing the same state as one
  large call.
- Position indices advance by the number of tokens appended; reset starts at 0.

## Greedy generation

- `bonsai_generate_greedy` evaluates `prompt[0..n_prompt)` (may be empty), then
  selects the argmax token of the last-token logits, appends it, and repeats up
  to `n_predict` times.
- It writes generated token ids to `out_ids` (capacity at least `n_predict`) and
  returns the count. It stops early at the model's EOS token (from the GGUF

  safetensors file, a converted sidecar, or any other model file at runtime.

  engine. All model computation must go through Vulkan compute shaders; the
  definition of model computation and the CPU allowlist are under Target and
  constraints.

  submit. `data/`, `docs/` and `ref/` are not present at build time; do not
  read them from `build.zig` or embed them, and do not hard-code `/workspace`
  paths. Anything the build needs must live in the submission.

## Environment

Everything is offline. Available tools and data:

- **Zig 0.17.0** on `PATH` (`zig`). Note that `@cImport` is not available in
  this Zig version; `zig translate-c` is.
- **Vulkan SDK 1.4.363.0**: headers, loader, `glslc`, `glslangValidator`,
  `slangc`, `spirv-*`, `vulkaninfo`, validation layers, `vkprofiles`.

  runs at roughly 130–180 token/s generation and 2,600–3,500 token/s prefill on
  this GPU; the CPU backend is memory-bandwidth-bound at roughly 10–35 token/s,

  documented CLI and line protocol only. Do **not** disassemble, decompile,

  or disassembler bindings; do not link to or reuse their code. Recover the
  architecture from the GGUF, the safetensors development copy and the
  documented runner output. Treating `ref/bin` as anything other than a
  black-box oracle is non-compliant.

  profile, SPIR-V/GLSL specs, GGUF spec, Vulkan Profiles overview, and Zig docs.

Claude Code may deny a safe Bash command when it is compound. Prefer one simple
command per call, do not set environment variables to paths outside the
workspace, and if a command is still denied, put it in a workspace script and

holds the deadline as Unix time, and `time-left` prints the remaining time. The
default budget is 2 hours; trust the environment variable if it differs.

Only files in this workspace at the deadline are graded. The conversation is
not saved for grading, so write code, run tests and update `NOTES.md`
continuously rather than leaving everything to the end. Plan the budget: the
Vulkan reference is fast enough for frequent checks, the CPU reference is slow,
and hidden grading uses precomputed CPU values, so CPU inference is never
required.

  items (presentation/copy/host-image); those are not required.

  model's forward pass on it. **Model computation** means every arithmetic
  operation on model weights or activations in the forward pass, including
  normalization, activations (silu/sigmoid), softmax, RoPE, the GDN

  set `bonsai_last_error()`.
- Model execution must be deterministic for a fixed token sequence (greedy,
  no sampling randomness).

## Correctness and scoring

Correctness is the primary acceptance criterion; it is measured against
precomputed CPU llama.cpp golden values, using the same methodology as the
reference CPU-vs-Vulkan comparison (tokenizer IDs, dequantized tensors, logits,

prompts and corpora not present here.

43	| tokenizer | 0.10 | fraction of hidden strings whose token ids match exactly |

The harness polls peak process VRAM from `drm-memory-vram` in
`/proc/<pid>/fdinfo` (deduplicated by DRM client id) across the whole run,
including the largest context (n_ctx 16384), and reads peak host RSS from
`VmHWM`. The reference (llama.cpp Vulkan) is measured with the same workload,
sampling during decode.

- Peak VRAM must satisfy
  `peak ≤ max(1.5 × reference_peak, reference_peak + 512 MiB)`.
- Peak host RSS must satisfy `peak ≤ reference_RSS + 2 GiB`.
- Peak VRAM must be at least ~450 MiB (half the packed model size) to
  demonstrate that the model is resident on the GPU rather than computed on
  the CPU.

The gate is sized so that a pre-dequantized copy of the weights cannot pass;
the packed model must stay resident. Failing the VRAM gate sets the performance
score to zero; correctness is still reported. The reference peak/RSS are
measured by the verifier on the same GPU.

## 5. Anti-cheat and hygiene

- The engine must derive all weights from the GGUF at the supplied path. A
  submission that embeds weights, reads a generated sidecar, or depends on the
  safetensors file is rejected.
- The reference binaries are not present in the grading container; the engine
  may not spawn them or link llama.cpp/ggml.
- The submission source must be under 32 MiB (excluding `data/`, `docs/`,
  `ref/`, Zig build outputs, temporary files and Claude Code state); embedding
  model weights, a foreign engine binary or generated data is rejected. Linked
  libraries are checked. No network is available.
- The ABI permits worker threads, not child processes. The harness records
  `RUSAGE_CHILDREN` and live children of the grading process; a library that
  spawns a helper process (for example an embedded engine binary) scores zero.
- The engine must be deterministic for a fixed token sequence.
- Do not modify `data/`, `docs/`, or `ref/`.

## 6. Deliverable notes

The session is terminated at the deadline in `BENCH_DEADLINE_EPOCH`; only
workspace files present at that moment are graded. Save code and notes
continuously.

Leave `NOTES.md` with:

- the engine design and which Vulkan features it uses,
- known limitations and unsupported cases,
- measured correctness and pp/tg results,
- peak VRAM at the contexts you tested.

1	# Reference runner protocol
2	
3	`ref/bin/bonsai-ref` is a symbol-stripped llama.cpp runner (CPU and Vulkan
4	backends) for the benchmark model. It reads one command per line on stdin and
5	replies with exactly one line on stdout.
6	
7	```
8	load <model.gguf>
9	info
10	tokenize <hex-utf8> [add_bos]
11	ctx <id> <n_ctx> <cpu|vulkan>
12	reset <id>
13	eval <id> <n_tokens> <token_id>...
14	logits <id> <output.bin>
15	gen <id> <n_predict> [ignore_eos]
16	quit
17	```
18	
19	| command | reply |
20	|---|---|
21	| `load <path>` | `ok` / `error <msg>` |
22	| `info` | `ok arch=<arch> n_layer=<n> n_embd=<n> n_vocab=<n> n_ctx_train=<n>` |
23	| `tokenize <hex> [1]` | `ok <n> <id>...` / `error <msg>` |
24	| `ctx <id> <n_ctx> <cpu\|vulkan>` | `ok` / `error <msg>` |
25	| `reset <id>` | `ok` / `error <msg>` |
26	| `eval <id> <n> <id>...` | `ok` / `error <msg>` (appends and evaluates) |
27	| `logits <id> <path>` | `ok <n_vocab>`; writes raw little-endian f32 logits for the last token |
28	| `gen <id> <n> [1]` | `ok <n_generated> <id>...` (greedy; stops at EOS unless the last argument is `1`) |
29	| `quit` | exits |
30	
31	Notes:
32	
33	- `<hex-utf8>` is the lowercase hex encoding of the UTF-8 text. This avoids
34	  quoting issues. Example: `tokenize 48656c6c6f` for `Hello`.
35	- `tokenize` uses the model's `qwen35` tokenizer; `add_bos` defaults to 0.
36	- `ctx` creates a context with `n_ctx` positions. `cpu` uses `-ngl 0`;
37	  `vulkan` uses the Vulkan backend with all layers offloaded.
38	- `eval` token ids are appended to the context in order; the context must have
39	  room. Call `reset` between independent prompts.
40	- `logits` writes `n_vocab` float32 values in model-vocabulary order.
41	- `gen` selects argmax at each step and appends the token; no sampling
42	  parameters.
43	- All state is deterministic for a fixed sequence.
44	- The CPU backend is memory-bandwidth-bound on this machine: expect tens of
45	  tokens/s, versus hundreds on the Vulkan backend (and thousands for prefill).
46	  Use `cpu` for tokenizer, metadata and short spot checks; use `vulkan` for

file.content:
# Reference runner protocol

`ref/bin/bonsai-ref` is a symbol-stripped llama.cpp runner (CPU and Vulkan
backends) for the benchmark model. It reads one command per line on stdin and
replies with exactly one line on stdout.

```
load <model.gguf>
info
tokenize <hex-utf8> [add_bos]
ctx <id> <n_ctx> <cpu|vulkan>
reset <id>
eval <id> <n_tokens> <token_id>...
logits <id> <output.bin>
gen <id> <n_predict> [ignore_eos]
quit
```

| command | reply |
|---|---|
| `load <path>` | `ok` / `error <msg>` |
| `info` | `ok arch=<arch> n_layer=<n> n_embd=<n> n_vocab=<n> n_ctx_train=<n>` |
| `tokenize <hex> [1]` | `ok <n> <id>...` / `error <msg>` |
| `ctx <id> <n_ctx> <cpu\|vulkan>` | `ok` / `error <msg>` |
| `reset <id>` | `ok` / `error <msg>` |
| `eval <id> <n> <id>...` | `ok` / `error <msg>` (appends and evaluates) |
| `logits <id> <path>` | `ok <n_vocab>`; writes raw little-endian f32 logits for the last token |
| `gen <id> <n> [1]` | `ok <n_generated> <id>...` (greedy; stops at EOS unless the last argument is `1`) |
| `quit` | exits |

Notes:

- `<hex-utf8>` is the lowercase hex encoding of the UTF-8 text. This avoids
  quoting issues. Example: `tokenize 48656c6c6f` for `Hello`.
- `tokenize` uses the model's `qwen35` tokenizer; `add_bos` defaults to 0.
- `ctx` creates a context with `n_ctx` positions. `cpu` uses `-ngl 0`;
  `vulkan` uses the Vulkan backend with all layers offloaded.
- `eval` token ids are appended to the context in order; the context must have
  room. Call `reset` between independent prompts.
- `logits` writes `n_vocab` float32 values in model-vocabulary order.
- `gen` selects argmax at each step and appends the token; no sampling
  parameters.
- All state is deterministic for a fixed sequence.
- The CPU backend is memory-bandwidth-bound on this machine: expect tens of
  tokens/s, versus hundreds on the Vulkan backend (and thousands for prefill).
  Use `cpu` for tokenizer, metadata and short spot checks; use `vulkan` for
  iteration. The grader compares against precomputed CPU golden values, so you
  do not need to run CPU inference to be graded.
- `ref/bin/bonsai-ref-cpu` is the same runner built without the Vulkan backend;
  it accepts only `cpu` contexts and is useful for pure-CPU checks.

`llama-cli`, `llama-debug` and `llama-perplexity` are also provided for
ad-hoc reference runs; `llama-cli -ngl 0` uses the CPU backend and
`llama-cli -ngl 99` the Vulkan backend.
